## Overall score: 68.8/100

### Record survives even if data is taken down (major gap)
You currently store your sample sheet only on the HPC storage volume, which means it would be lost if the volume were wiped. To fix this, you can assign a DOI to your dataset via a repository like Zenodo. This ensures a permanent record of your dataset's existence and metadata. This matters for health research data like yours because it allows for accountability and reproducibility, even if the original data is no longer accessible.

### Explicit reuse license or usage terms (unknown)
You can start by checking your dataset's metadata record or the documentation for your data-sharing agreement. If that doesn't have the information, you can reach out to whoever set up your repository account or your IT/data manager to see if they know about any license statements. They may be able to point you in the right direction or provide the necessary information.

### Discoverable somewhere searchable (minor gap)
You have a dataset listed in your internal HPC catalog, but it's not visible outside your team. To change this, you can assign a DOI via a repository like Zenodo. This will make your dataset discoverable to a broader audience. By doing so, you'll enable other researchers to find and build upon your work, which is crucial for advancing health research at an institution like yours.

### Metadata clearly identifies its dataset (minor gap)
You currently reference batch IDs in your metadata sheet, but not each sample's individual DOI. To fix this, you can assign a DOI to each sample via a repository like Zenodo. This will ensure that each sample's metadata is clearly linked to its corresponding data. Accurately linking metadata to individual samples is crucial for health research, as it enables precise tracking and verification of results.

### Defined access-control mechanism (minor gap)
You currently lack a formal process for revoking access to HPC cluster accounts when someone leaves the project. To address this, you can delegate the task of creating a simple access revocation workflow, possibly using an existing identity management tool. This matters for health data at your institution because it helps prevent unauthorized access to sensitive information. You can start by designating a person to review and update account access regularly.
